title: The Ethics of AI in Language Assessment

pts: AI systems increasingly score writing, and increasingly speaking, at meaningful scale, extending Unit 92's major-exam content into its most current development.
This capability continues to develop rapidly, meaning any specific description here will likely need updating relatively soon.
Understanding the genuine current capability, not hype in either direction, matters for informed professional engagement.

v: Five anonymized learner paragraphs; a free AI chatbot or writing-feedback tool; a rubric

items: Choose five short learner paragraphs with all names and identifying details removed; never upload identifiable learner work.
Score them with your usual rubric (Unit 46), without looking at any AI output.
Ask an AI tool to score the same paragraphs with the same rubric, and to give reasons.
Compare scores and reasons in a table.
Note where the tool agreed with you, where it differed and where its reasons were vague or wrong.
Repeat the same request to the AI tool twice and compare the two sets of scores for consistency.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A comparison table (fictional, written for this book):

lines: Paragraph 1: teacher 3/5, AI 4/5. AI reason: ‘varied vocabulary’. Teacher note: the argument is off-topic.
Paragraph 3: teacher 4/5, AI 3/5. AI reason: ‘informal expression “do the needful”’. Teacher note: an accepted Indian English phrase in a business email.
A: It agreed with me on three out of five.
B: And when it disagreed, it was looking at vocabulary and style, not whether the argument answered the question.

blocks.x: The aim is an honest picture of current capability, neither dismissive nor dazzled. Any description of specific tools will date quickly.

body: Purpose: to show a teacher comparing human and AI scores. Content: a teacher at a desk with a stack of scripts on one side and a laptop showing scores on the other; between them, a table with ticks for agreement and question marks for differences. Style: realistic, calm. Board version: a two-column table with ticks and question marks.

items: ChatGPT, Gemini or Microsoft Copilot (free tiers available, usage limits apply) for trial scoring.
Write & Improve from Cambridge (free) for automated feedback on learner writing [VERIFY current access].

blocks.x: Discuss a printed example of AI feedback prepared in advance by the facilitator.

pts: Does an AI scoring system genuinely measure communicative competence (Unit 27), or a narrower, more superficial pattern it has learned to detect?
This connects directly to Unit 92's construct-validity debate, now raised with additional urgency for AI-specific scoring systems.
This remains a genuinely open, actively researched question, not a settled one either way.

v: The comparison table from point 1; the four-competence rubric from Unit 46

items: For each AI score, identify the features the tool mentioned in its reasons.
Map each feature onto the four competences: grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic.
Identify which competences the tool attended to and which it ignored.
Write and try a ‘gaming test’: a paragraph designed to score well while communicating badly.
Try the same task with a spoken response, using a speech-scoring or pronunciation app.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A gaming paragraph (written for this book):

lines: Furthermore, the multifaceted ramifications of technological proliferation necessitate comprehensive, holistic paradigms; consequently, stakeholders must synergistically leverage innovative frameworks.
T: What does it say?
S1: Nothing, really.
S2: But it has long words and linking words. Let’s see what score it gets.

blocks.x: If a tool rewards this paragraph, it is measuring surface features, not communicative competence, a construct-validity problem (Williamson, Xi and Breyer 2012; Perelman 2014).

body: Purpose: to show the difference between surface features and the construct. Content: a large tree labelled ‘communicative competence’; a scanning beam from a machine lights up only the leaves (‘long words’, ‘linking words’, ‘length’), leaving the trunk and roots (‘meaning’, ‘appropriacy’, ‘argument’) in shadow. Style: clear diagram. Board version: a tree with some parts shaded.

items: Any free AI chatbot from point 1.

blocks.x: Swap gaming paragraphs between groups and score them with the human rubric.

pts: AI systems trained on particular language varieties and demographic patterns can show systematic bias against other varieties or groups.
This connects directly to Unit 78's World Englishes content — AI systems trained predominantly on Inner Circle varieties may unfairly penalise other legitimate varieties.
This is a genuine, documented risk requiring active, ongoing mitigation, not a hypothetical concern.

v: Paired speaking or writing samples from different English varieties

items: Prepare pairs of responses of similar quality that differ mainly in variety features (for example, Indian English and British English idioms, or recordings in different accents).
Score each pair with an AI tool and with human raters.
Record whether the tool scores one variety systematically lower.
Discuss what learners would face if the tool were used for grading, and which features are errors rather than legitimate variety features (Unit 78).
Test speech recognition by having teachers from different regions read the same sentence into a dictation tool and comparing the transcripts.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A dictation test (fictional, written for this book):

lines: Sentence read: ‘Please revert by Thursday regarding the thirty-three vacancies.’
Teacher 1: transcribed correctly.
Teacher 2: ‘Please reward by Thursday regarding the thirty free vacancies.’
T: Was Teacher 2’s English unclear to any of us?
Ss: No.
T: Then the problem is in the machine, not the speaker.

blocks.x: Bias of this kind has been documented in commercial speech recognition (Koenecke et al. 2020) and in score differences across groups (Bridgeman, Trapani and Attali 2012). It needs active monitoring, not assumption.

body: Purpose: to illustrate recognition bias across varieties. Content: two speakers saying the same sentence; above one, a correct transcript; above the other, a garbled transcript; a balance scale between them tilts. Style: neutral, not mocking any speaker. Board version: two speech bubbles and a tilted line.

items: Google Docs voice typing (free) or a phone’s built-in dictation for the recognition test.

blocks.x: Teachers compare their own transcriptions of recorded speech, discussing differences.

points.sub: A genuine technical and ethical challenge
pts: Many AI scoring systems function as a genuine 'black box,' making it difficult to explain exactly why a specific score was given.
This connects directly to Unit 73's assessment ethics — learners arguably deserve to understand the basis for consequential scoring decisions.
This transparency challenge remains a genuine, active area of both technical development and ethical debate.

v: An AI-generated score and a teacher-written rubric score for the same text

items: Show learners two feedback reports on the same text: one from a teacher using a rubric, one from an AI tool.
Learners list what each report tells them about why the score was given.
Learners write three questions they would want answered before accepting a high-stakes score.
Discuss: do learners have a right to understand a consequential score? Link to Unit 73.
Learners role-play a meeting in which a candidate asks an exam board to explain a low score.
Support: provide question starters (Why did…? Which part…? How can I…?).
Challenge: learners draft a short ‘right to explanation’ policy for their school.

lines: Which sentences lowered my score?
Was my accent counted as a mistake?
Can a human check the score if I disagree?
A: Can you tell me why my speaking score was 5.0?
B: The system identified limited fluency.
A: Which parts? What should I improve?
B: I’m afraid the system doesn’t give details.

blocks.x: Many automated systems work as a ‘black box’. Explainability remains both a technical and an ethical challenge, and learners arguably deserve reasons for consequential decisions (Xi 2010).

body: Purpose: to show the transparency problem. Content: a learner’s essay going into a closed black box and a number coming out; beside it, a glass box where the rubric criteria can be seen working. Style: simple, symbolic. Board version: a solid square and a dotted square.

items: Google Forms (free) to collect learners’ questions anonymously.

blocks.x: Two printed reports and a question sheet.

points.sub: Why this matters more than routine feedback
pts: Unit 84 noted AI feedback's genuine value for low-stakes practice; high-stakes assessment (immigration, academic admission) raises fundamentally higher ethical stakes.
Errors or bias in low-stakes practice feedback are inconvenient; the same errors in high-stakes assessment can genuinely alter someone's life trajectory.
This distinction should directly inform how cautiously AI assessment is deployed across different stakes levels.

items: List all the assessment uses in your context, from quick classroom checks to board examinations and admissions tests.
Place them on a ladder from lowest to highest stakes.
For each rung, decide whether AI scoring is acceptable alone, acceptable with human review, or not acceptable.
Justify each decision in one sentence.
Compare with Unit 84, where AI feedback was welcomed for low-stakes practice.
Add a column: ‘What if the AI is wrong?’
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A group’s stakes ladder (written for this book):

lines: Low: practice paragraph feedback at home. AI alone acceptable, with teacher spot-checks.
Medium: unit test contributing to the progress card. AI suggestion plus teacher decision.
High: selection for a scholarship or a visa-related test. AI only with human review and a clear appeal route.

blocks.x: An error in practice feedback is inconvenient; the same error in a high-stakes decision can change a life. Caution should rise with stakes.

body: Purpose: to show caution increasing with stakes. Content: a ladder with five rungs, from ‘practice’ at the bottom to ‘admission and migration’ at the top; beside each rung, a symbol for AI alone, AI plus human, or human decision. Style: clean infographic. Board version: a ladder with labels and symbols.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a printed stakes ladder.

blocks.x: The ladder drawn on chart paper for the staff room.

pts: Many current systems combine AI scoring with human review, particularly for consequential or borderline cases.
This reflects an appropriately cautious middle path between full automation and purely human-only assessment.
This connects to Unit 84's 'augmenting, not replacing' framing, applied specifically to this highest-stakes application.

v: A description of one AI-supported assessment process

items: Map the steps of an assessment process that uses AI scoring.
Identify where a human currently checks, and where none does.
Add checkpoints: random double-marking, review of borderline scores, review of unusual responses, and an appeal route.
Decide who is responsible at each checkpoint and how much time it needs.
Design lighter oversight for homework-only use.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An oversight plan (written for this book):

lines: 1. AI gives a provisional score. 2. Teacher double-marks one in ten scripts at random. 3. All scripts within one band of a pass boundary go to a teacher. 4. Any learner may request human re-marking. 5. Each term, compare AI and human scores by group to check for bias.

blocks.x: This follows the ‘augmenting, not replacing’ approach of Unit 84, applied to scoring.

body: Purpose: to show AI scoring embedded in human checks. Content: a flow diagram in which scripts pass through an AI box, then some are sampled or flagged and routed to a teacher; an appeal arrow runs back from the learner. Style: clear process diagram. Board version: boxes and arrows.

items: Google Sheets (free) to log AI and human scores and compare them.

blocks.x: A paper log of double-marked scripts.

body: Record both the AI score and the human score whenever you double-mark. Over a term, the log becomes evidence of how far the tool can be trusted for your learners, which is better than any vendor’s claim.

pts: Some institutions and jurisdictions are beginning to develop explicit policy around acceptable AI use in high-stakes assessment.
This connects directly to Unit 73's high-stakes-testing ethics — AI assessment governance is itself becoming a genuine policy question.
Staying informed about this evolving regulatory landscape is increasingly part of responsible professional practice.

v: School leaders, DIET faculty, teacher educators
Short summaries of the EU AI Act provisions on education, UNESCO guidance and the DPDP Act 2023

items: Groups read one summary each.
Groups note: what it requires, whom it protects and what it asks of institutions.
Groups compare: which requirements already apply in India, and which offer useful principles even where they do not apply?
Draft three lines for a school or DIET policy on AI in assessment.
Check whether your state education department has issued any circular on AI use and compare it with the summaries [VERIFY for your state].
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

Learners’ work is anonymized before any upload, and parents are informed of the tools used.

pts: Apply Unit 73's ethical framework directly: does this AI assessment tool serve learners' genuine interests, treat them fairly, and represent its own evidence honestly?
Advocate for transparency, bias mitigation, and appropriate human oversight wherever AI assessment tools are adopted in your own context.
This closes Tier IV's critical-awareness stretch, setting up the series' final, synthesising capstone.

v: A tool under consideration; a four-question checklist

items: Choose one AI assessment tool that your school uses or is considering.
Apply four questions: Does it serve learners’ interests? Is it fair across groups? Is it honest about its evidence? Is there human oversight?
For each question, list the evidence you have and the evidence you lack.
Decide: adopt, adopt with conditions, or do not adopt.
Write a short recommendation to colleagues.
Apply the same test to a non-AI assessment you already use, and compare.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: We recommend adopting the tool for homework feedback only. It helps learners revise, and early checks show reasonable agreement with teachers. We have no evidence yet about fairness for learners from Kannada- and Urdu-medium backgrounds, and the vendor does not explain its scores. We will not use it for grading until we have a term of double-marking data.

body: Before your school adopts any AI assessment tool, ask the provider three questions in writing: How was the system trained? How accurate is it for learners like ours? How can a learner challenge a score? Keep the answers, or the lack of them, on file.

aims.x: This unit closes the critical stretch of Part IV with a question that is only a few years old in its present form: what happens, ethically, when machines score language? Large language models and improved speech recognition now make it possible to score essays and spoken responses quickly and at scale. The unit examines what these systems do, what they may miss, whom they may treat unfairly, and how teachers and institutions can use them responsibly. Unit 84 explored AI as a support for learning; this unit concentrates on AI as a judge.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: describe, without hype in either direction, what automated language assessment currently does;
analyse whether an AI scoring system measures the construct it claims to measure;
explain how bias can enter automated scoring and whom it may affect;
evaluate the transparency of a scoring system and learners’ right to an explanation;
distinguish appropriate uses of AI scoring at low and high stakes;
describe models of human oversight in automated scoring;
locate current regulatory and institutional responses, including in India;
apply an ethical framework to decide whether and how to adopt an AI assessment tool.

why: Why this matters. Unit 84 introduced AI's opportunities broadly. Assessment specifically raises the highest-stakes ethical questions, given how directly it shapes real opportunities.

background.x: Automated essay scoring began with Ellis Page’s Project Essay Grade in the 1960s. From the late 1990s, systems such as ETS’s e-rater were used operationally alongside human raters in large-scale tests (Attali and Burstein 2006). Such systems predict human scores from measurable features such as length, vocabulary range, errors and discourse markers; speech scoring does the same with fluency and pronunciation. Several major English tests now use automated scoring for some or all of their writing and speaking components, sometimes with human review [VERIFY current practice of each named test before publication]. Generative AI has added a new layer: general-purpose chatbots can be asked to ‘mark this essay out of 10’, and many teachers and learners already do so.

The central professional question is validity, introduced in Unit 21 and developed for high-stakes tests in Units 73 and 92. Xiaoming Xi (2010) and David Williamson, Xi and F. Jay Breyer (2012) set out a framework for evaluating automated scoring: agreement with human raters is necessary but not sufficient; we must also ask whether the features the machine uses reflect the construct we care about, whether the system can be gamed, and whether it behaves fairly across groups. Les Perelman (2014) famously demonstrated that fluent-sounding nonsense could receive high automated scores, showing that a system can agree with humans on ordinary essays while measuring something narrower than communicative competence (Unit 27).

Fairness is the second concern. Brent Bridgeman, Catherine Trapani and Yigal Attali (2012) found that differences between human and machine scores varied by test takers’ country and ethnic group, and Allison Koenecke and colleagues (2020) found substantially higher error rates for Black American speakers than for white speakers in commercial speech-recognition systems. For Indian learners, whose English is a legitimate variety (Unit 78), the risk is that systems trained mostly on other varieties may misrecognize their speech or undervalue their writing. The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (AERA, APA and NCME 2014) require evidence of fairness for all intended test takers, and those requirements apply to machines as much as to humans.

Regulation is developing. The European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act (2024) classifies AI systems used to evaluate learning outcomes in education as high-risk, with obligations for risk management, transparency and human oversight. UNESCO (2023) has published guidance on generative AI in education and research, emphasizing human agency and age-appropriate use. In India, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 requires verifiable parental consent for processing children’s personal data, which matters whenever learners’ work is uploaded to an AI service [VERIFY implementing rules]. NEP 2020’s call for competency-based, formative assessment (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020) provides a further test: does an AI tool support that aim, or narrow it?

items: Comparison study. A table comparing human and AI scores on five anonymized texts, with a construct-validity commentary.
Bias check. A short report on a speech-recognition or scoring test across two or more varieties of English.
Oversight design. A process map for AI-supported assessment with human checkpoints and an appeal route.
Adoption recommendation. A recommendation on one tool using the four-question ethical test.
Have you used an AI tool to mark or give feedback? What did you trust, and what did you check?
Which of your assessments would you never hand to a machine? Why?
How would you explain an AI score to a learner or parent?
Whose English might an AI tool undervalue in your class?
How can your school stay informed as tools and regulations change?

terms.def: The policies, rules and oversight that decide how artificial intelligence tools are chosen, used and checked in an institution, including questions of transparency, fairness, data privacy and accountability for decisions.
Systematic unfairness in the output of an automated system, arising from its training data or design; for example, a scoring engine that marks down features typical of Indian English.
The use of software to assign scores to spoken or written performances; it raises questions of validity, fairness and transparency, especially when the scores inform important decisions.
An automated system whose internal workings cannot be seen or explained, so that users receive a result, such as a score, without reasons for it.
The extent to which a test measures the construct it claims to measure, and not other abilities; for example, whether a writing score reflects writing rather than typing speed.

Having two markers, human or human and machine, score the same piece of work independently, so that disagreements can be checked. It is used to monitor reliability and to keep human oversight of automated scoring.

The degree to which an automated system, such as an AI scoring tool, can give understandable reasons for its decisions. Many systems work as a ‘black box’, which raises fairness concerns in high-stakes assessment.
An assessment whose results have major consequences for the test-taker, such as admission, certification, employment or migration. Board examinations and international English tests are examples.
Keeping trained people responsible for checking and, where necessary, overriding automated decisions, such as AI-generated scores, especially in high-stakes assessment.

Technology that converts spoken language into text or responds to spoken input, used in dictation tools, voice assistants and pronunciation apps. Accuracy can vary with accent, so its feedback should be treated with care.
